Maladaptive Strategies.value: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

vignette:
Minh was forty-six, a software engineer who worked from a home office in a quiet suburban neighborhood, married to a woman who had learned to move through her own house with the soft-footed caution of a guest. Fifteen years earlier he had served as a scout in a mountainous region of Afghanistan, and one afternoon his unit had been ambushed while resupplying at a small forward post. He had been in a shower tent when the first mortar round hit—naked, vulnerable, unable to reach his weapon. The smell of burning diesel and scorched canvas filled his lungs. Then came the sound of a motorcycle engine revving, impossibly close, and the distinct crack of an AK-47. He scrambled out, grabbing a discarded pair of trousers, and spent the next two hours pinned behind a fuel barrel while rounds chewed the dirt beside him. He never spoke of that afternoon afterward, but the event refused to stay silent.

At home, the smells returned without warning. The charred edge of a neighbor’s barbecue, the sharp bite of gasoline at a pump—each odor yanked Minh into a memory so vivid he could hear the distant pop of gunfire in his ears. Those auditory flashbacks were not words; they were raw sound, a replaying film he could not stop. He had come to believe that if he let himself think about what happened, he would never pull free, so he learned to avoid anything that might start the reel. He stopped watching television dramas with war scenes, stopped browsing news sites with military coverage, stopped reading novels that mentioned combat. Going out became a calculated risk: he only drove familiar routes, never ventured into new neighborhoods, and felt a spike of cold alarm when a stranger approached him in a parking lot. Exercise, once a daily habit, also fell away—he found that the pounding of his own heart and the sense of physical exposure during a run left him feeling dangerously unguarded, as if he were back in that shower tent.

This vigilance followed him indoors. Even inside his locked home Minh was on guard, checking window latches twice, scanning the street before opening the front door for a delivery. The more he avoided, the more his world shrank, and the more his threat sense narrowed onto the few triggers he could not escape. A motorcycle passing under his window would send his pulse racing and drag the memory back, whole and sharp. He noticed that the act of avoiding—skipping a jog, turning off a film—left him more time to sit with the replay. The film played anyway, sound and all, and he could not put what he had witnessed into words. That inability to narrate the event deepened his sense of threat: he felt that if he could not explain it, he could never control it, and that helplessness made him even warier of unexpected smells or unfamiliar places.

Avoidance also reinforced his belief that the world outside was dangerous. By never going to new areas, he never disproved the danger, and the threat grew into a quiet certainty that strangers meant harm. Occasionally, when his wife suggested a weekend trip somewhere new, Minh felt a surge of panic that was not just fear but a kind of bodily knowing—the smell of unfamiliar air, the sound of an unknown engine—and he would refuse. He had begun to notice that the very effort to stay safe, to control his environment, made him more attuned to every possible cue: the whiff of something burning, the distant drone of a motor. The vigilance itself became a trigger, because being on guard sharpened his senses until ordinary smells and sounds struck him as warnings.

What finally brought Minh to a clinic was a moment of collapse at the grocery store. He had smelled grilled meat from the deli, heard a teenager rev his scooter in the parking lot, and found himself on the floor clutching his knees, unable to speak. His wife told him afterward that she could not keep living this way. Minh came because he was afraid—afraid that his marriage was crumbling, afraid that his work was suffering because he could no longer concentrate, and most of all afraid that the film would never stop playing. He did not know if talking could help, but he was certain that silence had not.
